title: THEIR OWN FATHER SOLD THEM. TWO SISTERS FINALLY EXPOSED THE SCANDAL.
paragraphs: THEIR OWN FATHER SOLD THEM. TWO SISTERS FINALLY EXPOSED THE SCANDAL.
They were supposed to be protected by their father. Instead, they became profitable transactions in his hands. But what their father exploited, God would weave into a story of redemption.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that comes from discovering that the person who was supposed to protect you was the very person taking advantage of you.
It hurts differently when betrayal carries your surname.
When the hands that should have sheltered you become the hands that exploit you. When the voice that should have defended your worth begins calculating what it can gain from you.
And perhaps one of the most disturbing conversations recorded in Genesis happened when two sisters finally spoke about what their own father had done to them.
Their names were Rachel and Leah.
Their father's name was Laban.
And their accusation was devastating.
“Are we not counted of him strangers? for he hath sold us, and hath quite devoured also our money.” — Genesis 31:15 (KJV)
Read that again.
Their own father.
Not a stranger. Not an enemy from another nation. Not someone who had entered their lives unexpectedly.
Their father.
The man whose household should have been their safest place had become a place where they felt like foreigners.
And the original Hebrew makes their accusation even more disturbing.
The phrase הֲלוֹא נָכְרִיּוֹת נֶחְשַׁבְנוּ לוֹ (halo nokhriyyot neḥshavnu lo) carries the meaning, “Are we not regarded by him as foreign women?”
Foreigners.
Outsiders.
Women who felt they no longer belonged in their own father's household.
Then comes the expression כִּי מְכָרָנוּ (ki mekharanu), meaning, “For he has sold us.”
The Hebrew verb comes from מָכַר (makhar), meaning to sell.
But their accusation did not end there.
They continued with וַיֹּאכַל גַּם־אָכוֹל אֶת־כַּסְפֵּנוּ (vayokhal gam-akhol et-kaspenu), an emphatic expression conveying that he had indeed consumed or devoured their money.
The repetition of the Hebrew verb for eating intensifies the accusation.
They were not simply complaining about an unpleasant father.
They were describing exploitation.
Laban had benefited from the arrangements surrounding their marriages, while his daughters believed they had been deprived of the financial benefits that should have been theirs.
To understand the weight of their words, we must go back to the night when everything changed.
Jacob had fallen in love with Rachel.
Genesis 29:20 tells us that he served Laban for seven years to marry her, and those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
Seven years.
Imagine waiting that long for the person you love, only to discover that the agreement had been manipulated.
On the wedding night, Laban gave Jacob Leah instead of Rachel.
When morning came, Jacob discovered the deception.
Laban defended his actions by appealing to the local custom that the younger daughter should not marry before the older.
Jacob was then permitted to marry Rachel after completing Leah's bridal week, in exchange for another seven years of service.
Fourteen years of labor connected to two marriages.
Although marriage arrangements involving bride-price or service existed in the ancient Near East, the existence of a cultural custom does not automatically make every use of it righteous.
And Genesis does not conceal the human suffering that followed.
Jacob felt deceived.
Leah lived with the pain of being less loved.
Rachel endured the anguish of infertility.
The sisters became rivals within a household fractured by favoritism, jealousy, competition, and desperation.
And Laban continued benefiting from Jacob's labor.
Years later, Jacob testified that he had served Laban for twenty years—fourteen for his daughters and six for his flock—and that Laban had changed his wages ten times.
Genesis 31:41.
This was not merely one unfortunate wedding night.
It was a pattern of behavior.
And perhaps that is why the words of Rachel and Leah are so powerful.
Two women who had spent years competing with each other finally stood together in recognizing what their father had done.
Sometimes the people you were taught to compete against are carrying wounds from the same source that wounded you.
Leah was not Rachel's deepest problem.
Rachel was not Leah's deepest problem.
They were two sisters living within a broken family system that had helped turn their relationship into a battlefield.
Neither woman was perfect. Scripture records their jealousy, rivalry, and flawed decisions.
But their imperfections did not make their father's exploitation acceptable.
And that distinction matters.
Because some people reading this have spent years believing that they must be completely innocent before they are allowed to acknowledge that someone has wronged them.
You can acknowledge your own sins without excusing someone else's.
You can repent of your bitterness without pretending the betrayal never happened.
You can forgive someone without calling their behavior righteous.
You can honor your parents without participating in their wrongdoing.
Biblical forgiveness is not the same as giving someone unlimited access to continue harming you.
And reconciliation is not the same as pretending trust has never been broken.
Jesus taught forgiveness, but He never taught that evil must be renamed goodness.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be valued only for what you can provide.
You became the dependable child.
The family provider.
The person everyone called when money was needed.
The one expected to sacrifice, understand, remain silent, and absorb every disappointment.
You gave until giving became an expectation.
You helped until your kindness became an entitlement.
And when you finally expressed your exhaustion, someone accused you of being selfish.
Maybe your story is not about money.
Maybe someone used your loyalty.
Your marriage.
Your generosity.
Your faith.
Your fear of disappointing God.
Perhaps someone even quoted Scripture to convince you that remaining silent about their wrongdoing was your Christian responsibility.
But God's Word was never given to protect exploitation.
It was given to reveal truth, expose sin, and lead sinners toward repentance and righteousness.
Ephesians 5:11 tells believers not to participate in the unfruitful works of darkness but rather to expose them.
And what happened next in Genesis is remarkable.
Before Rachel and Leah expressed their grievance, God had already instructed Jacob:
“Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred; and I will be with thee.” — Genesis 31:3 (KJV)
God had seen what was happening.
In Genesis 31:12, Jacob recounts God's words:
“For I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee.”
What a sentence.
I have seen.
The years of labor.
The manipulation.
The changed wages.
The unfair treatment.
Nothing had escaped God's knowledge.
And when Jacob explained God's instruction to return home, Rachel and Leah answered:
“For all the riches which God hath taken from our father, that is ours, and our children's: now then, whatsoever God hath said unto thee, do.” — Genesis 31:16 (KJV)
Their final words in that conversation deserve our attention.
כֹּל אֲשֶׁר אָמַר אֱלֹהִים אֵלֶיךָ עֲשֵׂה (kol asher amar Elohim elekha, aseh).
“Whatever God has said to you, do.”
They had acknowledged the injustice.
They had expressed their grievance.
And now they agreed to move forward in response to God's instruction.
Their story was no longer going to be defined entirely by what Laban wanted.
Yet Scripture remains remarkably honest about what followed.
Rachel secretly stole her father's household idols.
Jacob departed without informing Laban.
The family still carried unresolved struggles.
Leaving a broken environment did not instantly make everyone spiritually mature.
And that is something we often forget about healing.
A change of location is not necessarily a transformation of the heart.
You can leave the household that wounded you and still carry its habits.
You can escape manipulation and still struggle with controlling others.
You can recognize deception and still find yourself hiding behind lies.
You can survive betrayal and still need Jesus to heal the bitterness that betrayal planted within you.
The Gospel does not merely ask what happened to you.
It also confronts what sin is doing within you.
Because Jesus came not only to comfort wounded people but to save sinners.
And every one of us needs that salvation.
Including those who have been wounded.
Including those who have wounded others.
Including the Rachel, the Leah, the Jacob, and even the Laban within our own stories.
Now consider something extraordinary.
Leah—the woman who experienced the pain of being less loved—became the mother of Judah.
Genesis 29:35 records that when Judah was born, she declared:
“Now will I praise the LORD.”
The Hebrew name Judah, יְהוּדָה (Yehudah), is connected in the passage with the verb יָדָה (yadah), associated with giving thanks or praise.
And generations later, Matthew 1 records Judah within the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
The Messiah entered human history through a family line that included this deeply wounded woman.
The woman whose marriage began with deception.
The woman who longed to be loved.
The woman who stood beside her sister and accused their father of selling them.
God did not require a scandal-free family history before accomplishing His redemptive purposes.
He worked through broken people without endorsing their brokenness.
He accomplished His purposes without declaring their sins acceptable.
And He brought the Savior into a world desperately in need of grace.
Laban's exploitation was not righteous. But it could not overthrow God's redemptive purpose.
That is the difference between glorifying the scandal and glorifying the Redeemer.
We do not celebrate what happened to Leah.
We celebrate the God whose purposes were greater than the evil committed against her.
And centuries later, another betrayal would take place.
Jesus Christ would be handed over after Judas agreed to receive thirty pieces of silver.
Matthew 26:14–16.
The sinless Son of God would be betrayed, rejected, mocked, and crucified.
Yet through His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God would become available to all who repent and believe in Him.
First Peter 1:18–19 reminds believers that they were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
The Greek word ἐλυτρώθητε (elytrōthēte) means “you were redeemed” or “you were ransomed.”
And what was the price of that redemption?
Not money.
Not religious performance.
Not human approval.
The precious blood of Jesus Christ.
Do you understand what that means?
People may have treated you as though your worth depended on what they could extract from you.
But the Gospel reveals a Savior who gave Himself for sinners who could never purchase their own salvation.
Your redemption cannot be bought with another sacrifice of your own.
Christ has accomplished what you could never accomplish for yourself.

And perhaps tonight, beneath all your anger, exhaustion, and carefully concealed disappointment, what you really need is to stop trying to prove your worth to people and surrender your life to Jesus Christ.
Not because following Him guarantees that every earthly injustice will immediately be corrected.
Not because every stolen opportunity will necessarily be restored in this lifetime.
But because neither betrayal, poverty, rejection, nor the sins of another person can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
Romans 8:38–39.
Maybe you have been carrying a wound that nobody knows about.
Maybe you have spent years protecting the reputation of someone who never protected your heart.
Or perhaps, while reading this, you realized that you have been treating someone the way Laban treated his own family.
Using their generosity.
Manipulating their loyalty.
Taking advantage of their silence.
If that is you, do not use this story merely to identify the sins of other people.
Let it expose your own.
Repent.
Seek forgiveness.
Make restitution where possible.
Stop calling exploitation love.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not permission to continue harming people. It is an invitation to become a different person through Him.
You do not need to disclose private wounds publicly. But your simple confession may encourage another struggling soul to recognize that they are not alone in their need for Christ.
Your willingness to share biblical truth could help that person find encouragement, seek wise counsel, and turn toward Jesus.
We want to continue bringing Scripture into the places where people are hurting, confused, spiritually exhausted, and searching for truth.
Galatians 6:6 and 1 Corinthians 9:14 speak to this principle.
Not because salvation can be purchased.
And not because financial support is the only way to glorify Him.
But because generosity is one meaningful way believers can participate in the work of spreading biblical truth.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
If you believe this work is worth continuing, we warmly invite you to become part of it.
Never underestimate what God can accomplish through faithful acts of generosity, encouragement, and obedience.
Before you leave, remember Rachel and Leah.
Remember the two sisters who finally spoke about what their father had done.
Remember the woman who was less loved but became part of the family line through which the Messiah entered human history.
Remember that Scripture did not erase the scandal to tell the story of redemption.
And neither does the Gospel require you to pretend your past never happened.
Bring your wounds to Christ.
Bring your sins to Christ.
Bring your anger, your shame, your disappointments, and your need for forgiveness to Christ.
Your earthly story may contain chapters you wish had never been written.
But in Jesus Christ, there is forgiveness for the repentant, hope for the broken, and redemption for those who believe.
They may have put a price on what they could take from you, but Jesus gave His precious blood to redeem sinners like you and me.
The scandal may explain your scars, but it does not have the authority to write your eternity.
